video_title: Steady Global Economic Growth in 2027 Outlook But Risks Tilted to Downside
transcript: The global economy has held steady this  year, defying a war in the Middle East,   higher tariffs, and higher interest rates. But can  that resilience last? As we look forward to 2027,   investors are facing a new set of questions.  Will the AI boom cool down? Will higher borrowing   costs hurt growth? And will energy prices  remain a headwind or become a tailwind?   I'm Allison Nathan, and this is  Goldman Sachs Exchanges. Today,   we're diving into the economic and market outlook  for the year ahead. I'm joined by Jan Hatzius,   head of Goldman Sachs Research and the firm's  chief economist, and Dominic Wilson, a senior   advisor in the Global Markets Research Group. Jan, Dom, welcome back to the program.   Great to be here. Thank you.   I can't believe another year has gone by. Another  outlook report is out. Congratulations on getting   it out, and there's a lot to talk about. So, Jan, as I mentioned, between the war   in Iran, higher tariffs, higher rates,  you would've thought the global economy   would've struggled in 2026. But growth has  been relatively resilient. You've actually   described this year as remarkably unremarkable  in terms of growth. So, what's kept it going?   2026 has been a pretty good year, at least  globally. We are on track for growth of 2.7%   for the world economy. That's in line with our  estimate of potential, and it's not far from   what we thought at the start of the year. Some of the headwinds you mentioned have   been small. Tariffs, for example, were an  issue in 2025, but not really in 2026. We   did see an increase in interest rates, and  that, taken by itself, is a drag on growth.   But broader financial conditions have been  supportive of growth for most of the year.   And then if you look at the war in  Iran and the impact on energy prices,   that's been smaller than what you would have  perhaps expected given all the disruptions in   the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices did go up very  meaningfully, but not as much as some predicted,   and I certainly would have thought, if you'd given  me the entire chain of events in the Middle East.   And I think some of that is related to pipeline  redirection, some of it is related to dark flows   and escorted flows through the strait, and some  of it is related to reduced demand for oil, in   some sense, higher price elasticity in some parts  of the global economy, for example, in China.   And then you had a couple of significant  boosts to growth that have offset whatever   drag there was. I'd mention fiscal policy,  expansionary in the US on the back of the   2025 fiscal bill. In Germany on the back of  the defense and infrastructure program, and in   Asia in terms of fuel subsidies that insulated  household cash flow. So that's been helpful.   And then lastly, of course, we've seen a big  increase in AI investment throughout 2026. For   the year as a whole, we think we're getting an  increase that's worth about half a percent of   global GDP, and that's meaningful, even though, of  course, it's unequally distributed. You get a very   large growth boost in East Asia, especially Taiwan  and Korea. You get a moderate growth boost in the   US, and then something much smaller elsewhere.  But for the global numbers, it's been important.   But you expect some of those supports to fade in  2027, and you see risks to growth actually tilted   to the downside. So why the more cautious tone? The baseline is similar. We're at 2.8% for 2027,   and yes, we're seeing the financial conditions  boost fade, and probably replaced by at least   a moderate negative impact on growth over  the next few quarters, just based on what   our financial conditions indices have done. We're also probably going to get a more neutral   impulse from fiscal policy. But then there are  two things that are going to be helping us.   One, still ongoing strong growth in AI  investment. We do think that's probably   going to be front-loaded, so the biggest impact  in the early part of 2027. Then we would expect   that impact to fade as we go through the  year. But for the year as a whole, it looks   similar to 2026 in terms of the increase. And then we are expecting a friendlier backdrop   from an energy price and energy impact on real  income perspective. Our commodity strategists   have oil prices gradually coming down towards the  sort of $80 range in 2027. And that, combined with   the fact that we're going to be lapping the  biggest increases in oil prices, that should   actually help household income growth increase  in real terms. So, that gives us the baseline.   There are downside risks to the forecast.  And I would say number one, on oil prices,   we've seen much more positive near-term news flow  before, but there is still a risk that ultimately   we get an escalation, a renewed escalation and  renewed spike in prices that would certainly upend   some of the assumptions that we've been making. We are, I think, at risk of tightening in   financial conditions, for example, via spikes in  bond yields. Fiscal policy is on an unsustainable   path in a number of economies. I think that's  true in the United States, I think it's true in   the UK to a lesser degree, and then it's certainly  true in the Euro area, especially in France. We've   seen significant spikes in bond yields. We're  working our way towards the French presidential   election in April and May, and if investors don't  see a clear plan for adjusting fiscal policy,   then I think we're at risk of additional tensions  there, and that could also spill over into broader   financial conditions and slow growth. And then lastly, on AI investment, there   are a number of downside risks to this path of  continued increases. Some of those are regulatory,   pushback against data center investment, which is  something to be focused on. I don't expect a big   impact, but it's a very fluid situation  and obviously very politics-dependent.   There are a lot of shortages in the  semiconductor and especially memory industry,   which suggests that a significant chunk of  the increase in nominal spending could end up   going into price rather than volume, and that  would also be a downside risk for real GDP.   And then there's the question of, at what point is  the buildout of the AI capital stock sufficiently   advanced that you really see more of a slowdown  in demand? In our baseline, that doesn't happen   until 2028, 2029, but it's hard to time this, and  so I think that's another risk to be focused on.   Dom, let me bring you into the conversation.  We've just heard Jan's growth expectations:   pretty steady, stable, but with downside risks,  as he just spoke about. Are markets appropriately   pricing that risk? What do you make of this? Yeah, I think there's a similar balancing   act going on on the market side. The baseline  outlook that Jan laid out is pretty benign, and   our baseline is for positive equity returns, for  risk assets to be supported by that kind of growth   picture. I don't think we're obviously underpriced  to that growth view, but I do think it's a helpful   tailwind if that's where we're going. I think, like a lot of the last six months,   that means a lot of the action in markets is  going to be around these risks and the pricing   of the distribution of risks, and that's where  those opportunities are going to come from.   And I would say there are two that are still  very prominent: the oil and energy risk and   the AI theme, both of which Jan mentioned. I think  they operate on slightly different time horizons.   If you look at the energy risk, as Jan said,  the biggest near-term risk is probably that we   get renewed escalation and a renewed energy  price spike. I think what's happened is the   market has worried a lot about that coming into  the midterms. Our commodities team estimates   a risk premium in oil markets, which is how  far oil is trading above where we think the   fundamentals would put it. That was about $30 a  few weeks ago, as the worries about escalation   post-midterm were particularly high. We've seen  a lot of relaxation around that since that point.   We're close to zero on the risk premium now.  So, I would say in that sense, the market is   now more vulnerable again to that near-term  risk. Maybe that risk is a little underpriced.   I think the bigger story, which Jan focused  on, is how the market handles the transition   in the AI story and the potential peaking  of the growth impulse there. And I do think   relative to the economic story, that's a tougher  thing for the market story, for two reasons.   The first is that the contributions that the AI  investment story has made to CapEx, to earnings,   to market value are quite a lot higher than to  overall GDP growth in the US in particular. So,   it's just been a bigger issue for markets  than for the macroeconomy, and so there's   more focus on those dynamics in the markets. The second thing is that a peak in growth rates,   what we think of as a second-derivative turning  point, we've found historically tends to matter   more for markets. It allows markets to place  a limit on the upsides of distributions,   so even if growth stays strong, the slowing  or the peaking of that growth rate matters.   I think the market's been doing a lot of that  work. The good news is we've been de-rating   this AI area, particularly the infrastructure  producers, for a few months, so valuations are   less demanding. I think the bigger focus is now  going to be on the earnings side. We've had a   very sharp increase in the share of earnings, as  a proportion of GDP, going to S&P 500 companies.   That's been very supportive, but the big question  is how much of that is really sustainable   as the investment cycle peaks and fades. There are two reasons, I think, to be more   optimistic about that transition. One is that,  as Jan mentioned, the absolute rates of growth.   We're going to have positive CapEx growth. We re  going to have positive earnings growth, so even   if you're slowing to some degree, that impulse is  still positive, and that should be helpful. That   keeps valuations in check as well. The other is  that there may be a kind of baton-passing from the   people in the infrastructure providers, who have  benefited a lot, to some of the other parts of the   economy, hyperscalers or the broader economy,  in terms of who is benefiting from the boom.   So our base case is that this will be a more  benign version of that transition. But if   you think of the risks, the risk is that some of  these bigger aggregate shocks, energy, financial   conditions, or just the market pulling forward  that AI slowdown that's sitting further out,   that those have a bigger impact. We're priced  well for the baseline. On those downside risks,   we're still vulnerable in terms of the  way the market's priced at the moment.   Right. And while I asked you to focus on  the downside risks, our mainline views are   generally optimistic and steady growth. So  just to be perfectly clear, your mainline   expectations for asset markets is more upside. Yeah. So the mainline expectation's positive   for equities, and that is supported. The returns  are less dramatic than we've seen for some of the   last three years, but positive, and that positive  baseline growth story and some of what we think   on the inflation and policy side are important  underpinnings to that. But what I would say is,   if we get the risk cases, the market  obviously has some vulnerability to those.   We'll dig a little bit more into that in  a few minutes. But Jan, let me turn back   to you and ask about jobs, always in focus.  The labor market looks pretty solid. We got   another relatively solid upside surprise  on payrolls in the US, at least recently.   But AI does seem to be showing up a little bit  more in the numbers. So talk to us about that   and the risks to the job market from AI. Yeah. It's a similar story to what we've   been discussing. I think the baseline is one in  which the unemployment rate stays low and pretty   stable. We're at 4.1%, 4.2%, and we've been there  really for the US since June. Our expectation for   2027 is also in that range. That shouldn't be  surprising when the economy grows at 2% to 2.5%,   that s our estimate of potential growth. You  should see the unemployment rate be stable.   Underneath the surface, we are starting  to see somewhat more effects from AI. Our   expectation over the next several years  is that those effects are going to grow,   and we'll get a temporary increase in the  unemployment rate, or maybe a frictional increase,   in the unemployment rate of something like half  a percentage point, going into the 2028, 2029,   early 2030s period. And that's really based on  research that we and others have done that looks   at historical positive productivity shocks  and what those shocks do to unemployment.   And you typically get a temporary increase. We're in the very early stages of that, we think.   We have now seen over the past several months,  unlike a year or two ago, we have now seen a bit   more broadening out of the relationship between  AI adoption at the industry level and weaker labor   market outcomes. There's now a correlation across  industries between higher AI adoption and slower   employment growth, and also between higher AI  adoption and a somewhat higher unemployment rate.   Obviously, it's not dramatic, otherwise we  wouldn't be printing these strong headline   numbers. And there are also offsets from other  sectors, for example, data center construction.   But it is something that we're focused on as an  important development and probably also a downside   risk to the employment outlook as we go through  2027 and into the later part of the decade.   Yeah, very interesting. I do feel like our  conversation last year, we weren't seeing it,   and now we are. So very interesting to note. Let's turn to inflation. Again, very much in   focus. It has surprised sharply to the upside this  year in the US in particular. We just got another   unfriendly report this week, maybe some slightly  better data today. But in general, concerning on   the inflation side. Will it remain sticky, and  how are the risks to your inflation views skewed?   So clearly, inflation has come in much higher than  we thought at the start of the year. I think most   of that is related to some of these temporary  shocks, especially the higher energy prices,   and that's obviously very visible  in terms of headline inflation.   But it's also fed through into core  inflation, especially in the US,   to a significant degree through  channels such as airline fares,   which have gone up very sharply on the back  of higher jet fuel prices. There's also still   basically residual pass-through from the tariff  increases. We're estimating that at the moment   that's still contributing about 40 basis points  to the year-on-year rate of core PCE inflation.   So, if we add up the pass-through  from tariffs and from energy prices,   we can explain most of the overshoot of core  PCE relative to the 2% target. We're in the   low 3s for core PCE, and obviously, that's  more than 100 basis points above the target.   But as we go into 2027, we think we'll see an  improvement, a very substantial improvement,   in part because the tariff pass-through fully  basically evaporates sometime in early 2027,   and in part because of this more benign view on  oil prices, and in particular, the year-on-year   change in oil prices, which will really become  more benign, especially starting in March and   April when we lap the outbreak of the war. I'd also note that other broader measures of   pressure on the economy, especially in the labor  market, still look very benign. The labor market   is, in our view, in balance. The unemployment  rate is low, but not too low, but consistent   with a balanced labor market. And wage growth has  continued to decelerate in the US. We're now in   the low to mid 3s on nominal wage growth, which  is very reassuring. So that gives us core PCE   inflation in the 2.4% range by the end of 2027. Maybe just briefly on other economies. In general,   the news flow on core inflation outside the US has  actually been pretty good. In a lot of economies,   you've seen lower-than-expected numbers for most  of 2026 on core. Canada has been very benign. The   euro area has generally been pretty benign. Even  in the UK, where inflation had been higher than   in most other DM economies, in general the  news flow has been better. And while we do   expect somewhat more pass-through from high energy  prices, for example, in airline fares in Europe,   in general our expectation is that we won't be too  far above the target on core inflation in 2027.   If you go back to the US for a moment and we  think about our mainline forecast, which is for   a decline in inflation, do you think the risks,  though, are tilted to the upside on inflation?   I think the risks are tilted to the upside,  in part because the risks to energy prices   are tilted to the upside. So when we look at the  range of scenarios from our commodity strategists,   the upside scenario is quite a bit further  from the baseline than the downside scenario,   and that's clearly a source of upside risk. Other than that, I could find areas of upside   risk, for example, some additional  increases in AI-related pricing,   and some sources of downside risk. I think  having the labor market and the softness   in wage and unit labor costs feed through more  to the overall core inflation numbers, I think   that's a potential area of benign surprises. Interesting. So we've talked about growth,   we've talked about inflation. Let's talk  about the Fed and other central banks,   always a tremendous focus. The conversation  around the Fed has really flipped. I was looking   again back at our views last year, and there  were expectations for rate cuts. Obviously,   now the question is how many times will the  Fed and potentially other central banks hike?   So, putting everything that you expect this year,  again in terms of growth and inflation together,   what are you expecting for the Fed  and other major central banks?   Yeah. The monetary policy path has been a big  surprise. We came into the year thinking we   could still get another couple of cuts, from  the adjustment that we saw downward in 2025.   But the sharp increase in inflation and  the war sort of upended that forecast.   The Fed ended up moving to a hike at the September  meeting. There is almost certainly a hike at the   December meeting. There's even been a discussion  about whether that hike is going to be 25 basis   points or 50 basis points. Our expectation is  that it's going to be 25 basis points. And then   probably the FOMC is going to signal additional  tightening for 2027 through the dot plot,   which is again due at the December FOMC meeting. We think there will be one additional hike in   early 2027, I think more likely at the March  meeting than at the January meeting, but   that's really dependent on the economic data. We  think that the next couple of inflation numbers,   for November and December, are likely to look more  friendly than what we had the last few months.   In that case, I think that supports the idea  that they wait until March to deliver the hike,   but it certainly could be January as well. Ultimately, we have a benign view on underlying   inflation. We do think that a lot of the  inflation overshoot that we're seeing at   the moment is related to these more temporary  forces, and that's going to cap the amount of   tightening from the Fed at a level that's  less than what markets are pricing now.   But obviously, it's going to ultimately depend on  the data, because right now what you're hearing   from Fed officials is clearly more hawkish than  what we were hearing a few months ago, because the   numbers have come in higher. So time will tell. And what about the other major central banks?   I would say the theme is very similar that  markets are pricing more aggressive rate   increases than what we think is likely. As far as the European Central Bank goes,   we have a hike at the December meeting, and  then there's risk of another move in 2027,   but it's not our baseline. So that's  clearly less than what markets are pricing.   Similar story, I would say,  in the UK: one hike from here,   in this case in early 2027. So it's a similar  theme, that we think markets are putting too   much weight on what we think are ultimately  temporary upward pressures on inflation.   One outlier is the Bank of Japan, where  we're looking for three hikes from here   to a terminal rate of 2%, and that's actually at  or a little bit above current market pricing.   Dom, bond yield volatility has been a major  focus of the markets. What does everything   we ve been discussion about inflation, about  the central banks, and the Fed in particular,   mean for bond yields from here which again  are rising in the last couple of days.   And what would be the broader asset implications  if we stay at these higher bond yields?   Yeah, look, as Jan said, the most obvious  implication on our baseline view is that   our policy views are more benign than the  market in general. The fact that we have   a friendlier inflation backdrop and a  friendlier policy backdrop means that   the baseline story is more friendly for bonds  and for broader markets through that channel.   For government bonds, as you said, 2026 has  been a difficult year. They've essentially   been risk-additive for most of the year, with  yields going up as equities go down. We think,   certainly on that baseline, that 2027 is going  to be a friendlier year, and I think there   are a couple of things that are going on. First, just in terms of the starting point,   you have these higher yields going into it. Your  running yield is higher, and so that gives you a   decent buffer in terms of the returns you can  get out of a bond. But I would say also with   the inflation and policy views that we have, we  also have a gradual decline in those yield levels,   so in principle, on that path, you're going  to get a bit of capital appreciation out of   your bonds too, I think probably more likely as  the year progresses and some of those tailwinds   become more visible. So the overall environment  for bond returns is, I think, as positive as   we've seen it since 2020 on the forecasts. I think the additional thing that has been   shifting, which plays into the risks  and also the risks of higher yields,   is that mostly this year the risks have been  heavily tilted in terms of inflation and policy   shifts. The market got hit with the energy shock.  It got hit with a tightening cycle that it wasn't   expecting. Those risks are still there. We're  in the middle of the hiking cycle. As Jan said,   upside risk to energy gives you an upside skew to  the inflation forecast, so there's vulnerability   to that. And I think particularly in the next  few months, we're going to be wrestling with that   issue still, again with a bigger cushion against  it because of the way the market's pricing.   But definetely we're still seeing  scope for some upward risk to yields,   and in general that has been a brake on asset  markets. It's been a headwind for equities.   Those risks we've been dealing with most of  this year, and I think you're starting from   a better place. Those risks are still there. But as we move through the year, if you think   of the risks that Jan started with, I think  what's happening is that more of those risks   over time are shifting towards things that might  ultimately bring yields lower. If you think of the   AI-related risks, both investment slowing but  also job market risks from that front. If you   think of the financial stresses that could come  out of just higher rates in general, which we've   seen now a little bit of, the sovereign risks  from France and some other places, any of the   fiscal risks showing up as pressure to tighten. And so on bonds, I think, look, when we look at   the balance of risks, there's more diversification  benefit in terms of things that could drive yields   lower than has been the case this year.  We think that's probably something that's   shifting slowly. The upside risks are still  there, but the more you extend that horizon,   the more valuable. You're getting a better  yield, but you're also getting better protection   against some of these bigger risks from bonds. So I think it's going to be choppy. It's going   to be, I think, still a complicated picture, but  our view is generally a better picture than 2026.   Before we wrap up, Dom, a moment on the  dollar. What does all of this mean for   the outlook for the dollar? Yeah, the dollar, I think,   has a little bit of the same flavor as the bond  market story. Coming into this year, the energy   shock and the shift to tightening from the Fed  have been relatively supportive for the dollar,   at least compared to where we were going into  2025, with that long depreciation in the dollar   that we saw then. So we've had a range-bound  dollar for most of this year, but we're up at the   top endd of that with those supportive forces. Again, on the baseline, our view is that we're   going to go back to some softening in the  dollar. That's because that energy force   should fade, and some of those Fed risks should  fade out of the picture. That's probably most   clearly true against some of the undervalued Asian  currencies, the Japanese yen and the Chinese yuan,   for slightly different reasons. Both look  cheap to us. You have a big trade surplus   support for China. You have the policy rate  support now in Japan, and also some of the   shifting in the relative policy cycles there. The euro is a little bit more complicated.   Certainly over the next few months, we're dealing  with the risks from energy, and we're dealing with   some of the risks coming from the French election.  We've thought of the euro as a funding currency,   and I think that's probably still true,  at least in the more immediate future.   But I think some modest softening of the  dollar is more likely through the year.   I think again going back to what we've said  on a number of occasions, the AI theme and   how that plays out is going to be important.  Part of the premium that we've built into the   dollar has been this sort of tech exceptionalism  and the very big inflows that have come into the   US equity market on the back of that theme. The  more that holds up, the more sort of we're on the   very positive path there, the more support we'll  continue to give to the dollar. But any of those   stories where the market starts to look through  that, that AI investment impulse starts to fade,   that's where you could get a clearer weakening  than we've got in our forecasts. I would   say that just makes the dollar a bit more  cyclical around that axis than we've seen.   Jan, just to wrap up, what are you watching right  now to understand better whether any of these   downside risks are starting to materialize? It's really back to the three things   that are most in focus. One, what's happening in terms   of Middle East relaxation or renewed escalation,  and what does that mean for the energy impulse?   That's really important for both the growth  side and especially the inflation side.   Number two, what are we seeing on fiscal issues,  tensions in the next several months going into the   French election? I think that's a big focus. And then everything related to AI investment   and labor market effects. And there's a lot of  news that we'll probably learn over just the   next couple of quarters. We are expecting to see  ongoing increases over the next few quarters, but   then a deceleration as we go into the later part  of the year. And of course, every labor market   release we're going to scrutinize to see whether  there's more evidence for AI-related changes.   So, Dom, given what Jan just said, and our  mainline views which are relatively optimistic,   how should investors be thinking  about the landscape in 2027?   ? Yeah, look the baseline scenario we have, is  a pretty comfortable one. We're expecting out of   that positive returns in equities not as positive  as some of the very big returns in the recent   years but decent. We're expecting positive returns  on bonds. A little bit of underperformance in   credit, but nothing too dramatic. And commodities  delivering a flattish kind of return profile. But   the overall picture is pretty friendly. But I do think, to a greater extent than   is normally true, thinking about those  risks and making sure that portfolios   are positioned in a way that is not vulnerable  to those is a bigger deal than it has been.   And I would say specifically, I think that's  true tactically. We've found already over the   last few months that looking at where  we are in terms of the pricing of the   risk around AI and energy, as the market  swung pretty hard backwards and forwards,   gives you quite a good sense of where some of  the opportunities are coming, month by month.   Structurally, I would say there are  two things that come out of that.   One is diversification. As I said, bonds are  a better diversifier for equities against some   of these risks than they have been. And energy,  although we're forecasting pretty low commodity   returns, slightly negative, in fact, in the  baseline for 2027, we think still offers a lot   of value in a portfolio because of that upside  tail risk that we're still worried about.   And then explicitly hedging portfolios.  I think just in very general terms,   equity index volatility has stayed relatively low.  We think it's more likely to go up than down. We   think options protection for portfolios. Lots  of different ways you can do that, is probably,   again, more valuable in this kind of environment  with this sort of uncertainty than before. And   some of these positions, either for higher energy  prices, lots of different ways to do that too,   or for much lower rates, in case some  of these broader growth risks come down,   are also things that are worth considering. So I would say it's a comfortable baseline,   but much more than before, you need to be careful,  you need to be focused on those risks. And I think   people should make sure that portfolios  are adequately set up to deal with them.   Jan, Dom, thanks so much for joining us. Thank you.   Thank you. This episode of   Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Friday,  November 13th, 2026. If you enjoyed the show,   we hope you'll subscribe on Apple Podcasts,  Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts,   and leave us a rating and comment. I'm Allison  Nathan. Thanks for listening.
